analysis.one_liner: Requires EPA to charge large electricity-consuming facilities for their annual power use.
analysis.headline: A bill to charge certain large facilities for the electricity they use was introduced in the House on September 16, 2026 and referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, with no cosponsors and no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Clean Air Act to require the Environmental Protection Agency to impose and collect a charge on the total annual electricity consumption of certain facilities, paid by the owners or operators of those facilities [S1]. The design puts the cost on a narrow set of large electricity users rather than on all utility customers. The bill was introduced late in the 119th Congress, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and has no cosponsors [S1][S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary utility customers stand to benefit if the charge shifts the cost of very large electricity users away from the general rate base, and if it discourages facilities from adding demand that strains the grid and drives up everyone's rates. The EPA would also gain a new funding and enforcement lever under the Clean Air Act.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to impose and collect a charge on the total annual electricity consumption of certain facilities, with the charge paid by the facility's owners or operators [S1].
Places the charge within the Clean Air Act, linking electricity demand at large facilities to the federal air-pollution framework [S1].
Directs the cost at a specific class of large users rather than spreading it across all electricity customers, whose rates often rise when very large loads connect to the grid.

analysis.who_pays: The owners and operators of the covered facilities, who would pay a charge on every unit of electricity their facilities consume each year. If those facilities pass the charge along, it could show up in the prices of whatever they produce.

drawbacks.text: A new federal charge on electricity use is a new cost for covered facilities, and facilities under competitive pressure may pass some of it to their customers in the form of higher prices [S1].

The bill applies to 'certain facilities' as defined in the bill text; a charge aimed at very large electricity users is a narrow intervention that does not address the broader causes of rising electricity demand or rates.

Charging large users for electricity they already lawfully buy could be challenged as duplicative of state utility regulation, and the revenue purpose under the Clean Air Act framework is not laid out in the available material.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If the covered facilities are indeed very large electricity users, the case for the bill is that they impose real costs on the grid and on other ratepayers and should bear more of them directly; the cost is a new federal charge that could be passed through to consumers of whatever those facilities produce. The available material does not include the bill text or a CRS summary, so the definition of 'certain facilities,' the charge's size, and what happens to the money are not established here, and any weighing must carry that uncertainty.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no further action; it has no cosponsors and Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on September 16, 2026 [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and no further action has been taken [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: At this stage nobody has won anything: no large electricity users are paying a charge, and household utility customers have not gained the protections the bill would offer. The status quo — in which large facilities' grid costs are not charged by the federal government — continues, which favors the covered facilities.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Covered large electricity users, for now

for.name: Rep. Paul Tonko
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.

sides.party_line_note: There have been no votes and no cosponsors, so the partisan shape is unknown; the bill has a single Democratic sponsor and no Republican support on the record [S2].

industries.industry: Data centers and other very large electricity consumers
industries.note: If the covered facilities include hyperscale electricity users, the bill would put a federal charge on every unit of power they consume, a direct new cost their industry would resist. The bill's premise is that their outsized electricity demand imposes costs on everyone else's rates and on air quality.

The charge is collected by the EPA on facility owners, so utilities do not pay it directly. Utilities could benefit indirectly if very large loads are charged for the grid strain they cause, since that strain otherwise drives up rates for all customers.

analysis.trajectory: With one sponsor, zero cosponsors, and only weeks remaining in the 119th Congress, the bill is very unlikely to receive a markup or a floor vote; the overwhelmingly common path for a first-day introduction with no cosponsors is to remain in committee until the Congress ends in January 2027.
